analysis.one_liner: Lets cities regulate cable TV rates again and requires cable systems to carry local broadcast stations.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after four subcommittee hearings, the House Energy and Commerce Committee never acted on it, and it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 1984 Cable Act deregulated cable rates, the bill's own findings state that basic cable rates rose sharply — up 40% or more for 28% of subscribers in some markets — while most subscribers had only one cable company to choose from [S3]. The bill would let local franchise authorities cap basic cable rates where the cable system faced no effective competition [S2][S3]. It would also require cable operators to carry local broadcast and public-television stations, ban pay-for-carriage, stop cable operators from owning more than 15% of all cable subscribers nationwide, bar cable-affiliated programmers from discriminating against rival distributors, and make it easier for cities to deny franchise renewals to poor performers [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Cable subscribers, who would regain local rate regulation where their cable company faces no real competition [S2][S3]. Viewers who depend on free over-the-air broadcast stations, including public educational stations, since cable operators would have to carry local signals on the lowest-priced basic tier without degrading them or moving them to bad channel positions [S2][S3]. Local governments, which would get clearer power to enforce franchise standards and protection from unlimited damages claims when they regulate cable [S2][S3]. Rival video distributors such as satellite and wireless operators, which could no longer be charged discriminatory prices by cable-affiliated programmers [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Restores local authority to regulate basic cable rates and equipment charges wherever the cable system is not subject to effective competition, reversing the near-total rate deregulation that followed the 1984 Cable Act [S2][S3].

Requires cable operators relying on the compulsory copyright license to carry a set number of local broadcast stations — scaled to their channel count — on the lowest-priced basic tier, at full signal quality, with 30 days' notice before deleting or repositioning a station, and bars accepting payment for carriage [S2][S3].
Mandates carriage of at least one or two noncommercial educational (public television) stations per system, protecting access to public broadcasting for subscribers [S2][S3].

Caps any cable operator's share of the national cable market at 15% of subscribers, with existing large operators required to sell down within one year, to counter industry concentration and vertical integration [S2][S3].

Bars cable-affiliated programmers from discriminating in price, terms, or availability against other distributors, opening programming access for satellite and other competitors — competition that would pressure cable rates [S2][S3].

Overhauls franchise renewals so cities must hold open proceedings, invite competing franchise proposals, and can deny renewal to operators with poor service, complaint response, or billing practices [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Cable operators, which would face rate regulation, mandatory carriage of local and public stations on their basic tier, a 15% national ownership cap, and stricter franchise renewal review [S2][S3]. Vertically integrated cable programmers, which could no longer charge rival distributors discriminatory prices [S2][S3]. Some compliance costs would ultimately flow into subscriber bills or channel lineups, and rate-regulated systems could have less incentive to invest in upgrades.

drawbacks.text: Rate regulation risks suppressing investment in network upgrades and new services; the bill's own findings note cable was the most efficient distribution system and that regulation could chill the capital spending that added channels to subscribers' lineups [S3].

Mandatory carriage occupies cable channels — as many as one-third of usable channels for large systems — which can crowd out new programming services the bill itself says concentration was blocking [S3].

The bill limits relief in First Amendment suits against franchising authorities to injunctions, declaratory orders, and attorney's fees, which protects cities from damages but also narrows the remedy available to operators and others who challenge franchise decisions [S2][S3].
The 15% national ownership cap is a blunt tool applied to all operators regardless of local market power, and incumbents over the cap could keep their position for a year before selling down [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer case was strong by the bill's own record: rates up roughly three times faster than inflation after deregulation, 28% of subscribers facing 40%+ increases, and most subscribers with no second cable provider to choose from [S3]. Restoring rate regulation where competition is absent, guaranteeing carriage of local news and public stations, and opening programming access for competitors all address that directly [S2][S3]. The main honest costs are the risk that rate caps slow network investment, that must-carry crowds out new channels, and that the ownership cap is a crude instrument [S3]. On balance the benefits to subscribers outweigh the costs, though the rate-regulation design left real room for the regulatory inefficiency opponents feared.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, whose telecommunications subcommittee held four hearings on it in 1990 but the full committee never voted it out, so it never reached the House floor and died when Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Cooper introduced the Cable Television Consumer Protection Act of 1989 on November 21, 1989, with Rep. Christopher Shays, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S3][S5].
It got one Republican cosponsor and was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance in December 1989 [S4][S5].
The subcommittee held hearings on March 1, April 19, May 9, and May 16, 1990, but the full Energy and Commerce Committee never reported the bill to the House [S5].
No floor vote, no Senate action, and no further committee action followed before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The cable industry. Cable operators kept the rate deregulation that had produced the 40% increases in basic rates documented in the bill's findings, faced no must-carry mandate, no 15% ownership cap, and no easier path to franchise revocation — and cable subscribers kept paying the resulting rates [S3][S5].

for.name: Rep. Jim Cooper
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 21, 1989, to restore local cable rate regulation and mandate carriage of local broadcast signals [S1][S3].

for.name: Rep. Christopher Shays
for.what_they_did: Joined Cooper in introducing the bill, the bill's only cosponsor [S3][S4].

for.name: Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance, House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Held four hearings on the bill between March and May 1990 but never produced a bill to the full committee [S5].

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (chaired by Rep. John Dingell, D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill to the House after its subcommittee's hearings; the bill died in committee [S5].

against.name: Cable television industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed rate re-regulation, must-carry mandates, and ownership caps during the late-1980s cable policy debate; the bill's findings directly target industry rate increases, concentration, and vertical integration [S3].

sides.party_line_note: No recorded votes exist to measure party splits; the bill was sponsored by a Democrat with a single Republican cosponsor and died in committee without any chamber action [S1][S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would reimpose local rate regulation on systems without effective competition, force carriage of local and public stations on the basic tier, cap national ownership at 15%, and make poor-performing operators vulnerable to losing franchises [S2][S3]. Its gains would come at the direct expense of the roughly 56% of TV households who subscribed to cable [S3].

Cable-affiliated programmers could no longer discriminate in price or availability against rival cable systems and other multichannel distributors, ending a lever that favored affiliated systems and blocked competitors [S2][S3].
Guaranteed carriage on basic cable protects stations' viewership and advertising revenue as cable grows — the same local news and free programming that subscribers and non-subscribers rely on [S3].
At least one or two public station signals would have to be carried on every covered cable system, nondiscretionarily, keeping public broadcasting reachable for subscribers [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Non-cable multichannel video distributors (satellite, MMDS, TVRO)
industries.note: The programming nondiscrimination rule would let these competing distributors buy cable-affiliated programming on fair terms, building real competition that could hold cable rates down [S2][S3].

Cities would regain authority over rates, technical standards, and franchise renewals, and get protection from unlimited damages in First Amendment suits over franchise decisions — a legal exposure the bill's findings said cities were unreasonably facing [S3].
